name: Mucusless diet

card.summary: A fruit-and-vegetable diet devised by Arnold Ehret in the early 1900s that avoids foods it calls mucus-forming, promoted for clearer skin and a 'cleansed' look.
card.note: Very restrictive; nutrition researchers note possible shortfalls in protein and vitamins, and fasting carries its own risks.

quick.overview:
The Mucusless Diet Healing System was formulated by the German naturopath Arnold Ehret, who taught that foods such as meat, dairy, eggs, grains and starches form mucus and cause illness. His programme centres on fruit, with raw or cooked non-starchy vegetables as a transition, plus fasting.

Followers say it clears the body of 'mucus' and shows in clearer skin and a leaner look. Mainstream critics describe the doctrine as unsupported by physiology and warn about nutrient gaps; no clinical trial has tested it.
quick.how: Practitioners describe moving in stages from a standard diet toward raw fruit and leafy vegetables, often with periodic fasting. Some online followers adopt it as a fruit-heavy or fasting-based approach to skin and body composition.
quick.risks: Critics note that a diet built mainly on fruit may lack adequate protein, fats and vitamins, and Ehret's own claims have been described as unsupported. Extended fasting carries risks including electrolyte disturbance. People with medical conditions, children and pregnant people are generally advised by clinicians to avoid very restrictive diets.

lead: The mucusless diet is the central teaching of Arnold Ehret (1866-1922), a German naturopath who published the Mucusless Diet Healing System in the early twentieth century. He taught that 'mucus-forming' foods, including meat, eggs, dairy, grains, legumes, potatoes and rice, cause disease, and that a mostly fruit diet combined with fasting restores health.[1]

In appearance communities it is cited by people who connect a 'cleansed' diet with clearer skin, a lean build and a bright complexion, a chain of reasoning that rests on followers' accounts rather than controlled study.[1]

Physicians and nutrition writers regard Ehret's explanations, including his account of white blood cells and mucus, as unsupported, and critics have called the diet nutritionally inadequate.[1] Ehret's writings gained a following in the 1960s among naturist and surf circles and were later revised by Paul Bragg.[1]

chain: Followers report clearer skin and leaner body
angle.text: Followers use the diet in the belief that removing mucus-forming foods improves skin clarity and body composition. A fruit-heavy, low-calorie pattern can reduce body weight, which is a separate effect from the mucus theory.

paras: Ehret was born in the Black Forest near Freiburg and trained as a drawing teacher. Poor health in the 1890s led him to naturopathy, fasting and a fruit-based diet. He founded sanitaria in Switzerland, moved to the United States in 1914 and opened an office in Los Angeles, where he died in October 1922.[1]

Ehret held that mucus-forming foods cause disease, that simple fruit sugars are the body's proper fuel, and that fasting cleanses. He rejected meat, eggs, dairy, fats, grains, legumes, potatoes and rice in favour of fruit.[1]

He also sold a laxative called Innerclean by mail order; an American Medical Association laboratory reported its contents as herbs such as senna with other residue, and US authorities seized cartons in 1931 for misbranding.[1]

Reviewers describe Ehret's claims as unsupported and say the diet lacks adequate protein and vitamins, while fasting has no demonstrated significant benefits.[1] A 1987 overview of vegetarian diets lists the related natural hygiene diet among the regimens and discusses nutritional concerns about calcium, iron and vitamin B12 in restrictive plant-based diets.[2]

timeline.event: Ehret moves to the United States.[1]
US authorities seize cartons of his Innerclean laxative for misbranding.[1]
